doc.title: Dave Frishberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

chapter: New York studio and sideman work
title: Jazz players and studio musicians
summary: Many studio players were versatile professionals rather than jazz players, and they often defined what the sessions required.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well a question I’ve been interested in is how much the jazz players played a role in creating that kind of pop music of the day. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
I don’t think they could create — for that day? I don’t know that they did at all.
I mean but they were in the studio doing a lot of the work.

Some of them were, some of them were. There were a lot of musicians who worked in the studios that weren’t really jazz musicians that were studio musicians and that was their specialty. And they played all different kinds of music and they were very, very versatile and they were the kinds of musicians that the producers and arrangers loved to have around. They were available with instant help with instant answers to things, with instant remedy for whatever you want. You want this beat? Klunk. You know. And they were the professional studio players. They were more than jazz players, they were broader than that.
Okay. They had to be able to do whatever was required at the drop of a hat and know different styles.
They often defined what was required. They were that influential and they were that powerful.
